question_text: Draw the schematic symbols for an NMOS and a PMOS transistor side by side.
answer_text: The NMOS typically has the arrow pointing OUT (or no bubble on the gate). The PMOS typically has the arrow pointing IN, or a tiny inversion bubble on the gate.
explanation_text: NMOS transistors are traditionally drawn with the body arrow pointing outward, representing the N-channel. PMOS transistors are drawn with the body arrow pointing inward. In digital logic schematics, you will often see them drawn simply as a line with a gate lead, where the PMOS has a small circle (inversion bubble) on its gate to indicate it is active-LOW.
bonus_question_text: Why do hardware designers heavily prefer NMOS over PMOS for high-power or high-efficiency applications?
bonus_answer_text: The charge carriers in an NMOS are electrons, while in a PMOS they are "holes." Electrons have much higher mobility than holes, meaning an NMOS has a significantly lower R_DS(on) and switches much faster than a PMOS of the exact same physical silicon size.
